text_blocks.snippet: Treatment options for hypertension (high blood pressure) combine heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when necessary, prescription medications to lower blood pressure below the target goal of 130/80 mm Hg for most adults.
snippet_highlighted_words: combine heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when necessary, prescription medications

text_blocks.snippet: Adopting healthy habits can lower blood pressure and reduce the number or dose of medications required:

list.snippet: DASH Eating Plan: Follow the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet, which emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while reducing sodium.

snippet_links.text: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)

list.snippet: Sodium Reduction: Limit daily salt intake (ideally aiming for under 1,500 to 2,000 mg per day).
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise, such as walking, cycling, or swimming.
Weight Management: Achieve and maintain a healthy body weight.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Reduce or eliminate alcohol consumption and avoid tobacco products, which constrict blood vessels.
Quality Sleep: Aim for at least 7 hours of sleep per night and address conditions like sleep apnea.

text_blocks.snippet: When lifestyle changes are not enough, healthcare providers prescribe one or more American Heart Association first-line drug classes:

list.snippet: Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) Inhibitors: Keep blood vessels from narrowing (e.g., lisinopril, ramipril).
Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Relax and widen blood vessels (e.g., losartan, valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells to promote relaxation (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem).
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the body eliminate excess sodium and water, with thiazide diuretics most commonly prescribed (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide).
Beta-Blockers: Lower heart rate and cardiac output; often used if you have coexisting heart failure or coronary artery disease (metoprolol, carvedilol).

Multi-Drug and Fixed-Dose Combinations: More than 50% of people with hypertension require two or more medications, often taken as a single-pill combination to improve blood pressure control and adherence.

Resistant Hypertension: If blood pressure remains high despite taking three or more drugs (including a diuretic), providers may adjust dosages, check for secondary causes, or use specialized options like mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists or renal denervation.

text_blocks.snippet: Guidance and safety resources are also provided through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
